prompt: What does Android's documentation say window size classes are not determined by?

choices.text: The window's width in dp
choices.why: The width in dp is exactly what they are determined by.

choices.text: The window's height
choices.why: Height has classes of its own: compact, medium and expanded.

choices.text: The size of the device's screen
choices.why: Right. They come from the window the app has, which can be part of the screen.

choices.text: Whether the app is in split screen
choices.why: Split screen changes the window, so it changes the class.

prompt: Which of these change the window an app is given, while it is running? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The user turns the phone
choices.why: Width and height swap.

choices.text: A foldable is opened
choices.why: The window jumps to nearly tablet size.

choices.text: The user drags the divider in split screen
choices.why: The app's share of the screen changes.

choices.text: The user raises the screen's brightness
choices.why: Brightness changes nothing about the window's size.

prompt: An app is locked to portrait. Why do Apple's guidelines still ask it to resize well?

choices.text: Windows change for other reasons too
choices.why: Right. Split screen, resizable windows and other displays still reach it.

choices.text: Because iPhones ignore the lock
choices.why: The lock works; the window changes for other reasons.

choices.text: Because portrait windows are all the same size
choices.why: They are not; phones differ, and split screen narrows them.

choices.text: Because store review rejects locked apps
choices.why: The lesson names no such rule.

prompt: An app decides its layout once at launch by checking whether the device is a tablet. Which situation does it get wrong?

choices.text: A phone that never leaves portrait
choices.why: That is the one case the check happens to handle.

choices.text: A tablet that is used in landscape all day
choices.why: The check says tablet and the window is wide; it happens to fit.

choices.text: An emulator on a laptop
choices.why: An emulator reports a device like any other.

choices.text: A tablet put into split screen later
choices.why: Right. The device is still a tablet, the window is now phone-sized, and the app never asks again.

prompt: At what width in dp does Android's expanded width class begin?
Match each window width to its Android width class.
How does iOS describe the space an app has?

choices.text: Five width classes with dp breakpoints
choices.why: That is Android's scheme.

choices.text: Compact or regular, on each axis
choices.why: Right. Four combinations, set by the device, the window and multitasking.

choices.text: As phone or tablet, from the device model
choices.why: The guidelines say not to decide layout from the device type.

choices.text: Portrait or landscape only
choices.why: The guidelines say orientation does not tell an app how much space it has.

prompt: A React Native screen reads useWindowDimensions(). When is it drawn again with new values?

choices.text: When the app is restarted
choices.why: It updates while the app runs.

choices.text: When the window or font scale changes
choices.why: Right. That is what its documentation says it updates on.

choices.text: Every 16.67 ms, on each frame
choices.why: It changes with the window, not with the frame clock.

choices.text: When the device is identified as a tablet
choices.why: It reports the window, and it never asks what the device is.

prompt: A phone in landscape is 800 dp wide and 360 dp tall. Why does Android's documentation warn against two panes there, though the width is not small?

choices.text: 800 dp is compact width
choices.why: 800 dp is medium; compact ends at 600.

choices.text: Landscape windows have no size class
choices.why: Every window has a width and a height class.

choices.text: Two panes are a tablet feature
choices.why: Nothing is allowed by device; the decision is about the window.

choices.text: Its height is compact
choices.why: Right. Under 480 dp tall, each pane would hold almost nothing.

prompt: Match each part of the planner to the kind of size it should have.

pairs.left: the new-session form on a tablet
pairs.right: fill up to a maximum, then centre

right_distractors: a fixed width in physical pixels

prompt: Why cap the width of the new-session form at 600 units rather than let it fill a tablet in landscape?

choices.text: A line across the whole screen is hard to read
choices.why: Right, and the space left over can hold something else.

choices.text: Compose cannot draw anything wider than 600 dp
choices.why: It can; the cap is a design choice.

choices.text: Wide text fields use more battery
choices.why: The cost is to reading, not to the battery.

choices.text: Touch targets wider than 600 units are refused
choices.why: Nothing refuses a wide target; 48 dp is a minimum.

prompt: When the user turns the phone, what happens to the app's window?

choices.text: Nothing; the screen rotates the picture
choices.why: The app is told about a new window and lays itself out again.

choices.text: It doubles in width
choices.why: It does not double; the two sides swap.

choices.text: Its width and height swap
choices.why: Right. Orientation is just a change of window.

choices.text: It keeps its size and gains a scroll bar
choices.why: The window really changes shape.

prompt: A student types half a session's title and turns the phone. The field comes back empty. Which of the lesson's three checks failed?

choices.text: The state survives the change
choices.why: Right. On Android the screen is rebuilt for the rotation, and the half-typed title is state.

choices.text: Nothing sits under the notch
choices.why: A notch hides content; it does not erase it.

choices.text: The touch targets stay 48 dp
choices.why: That is not one of the three, and it would not empty a field.

choices.text: The content fits the short side
choices.why: The field was drawn; it was its contents that were lost.

prompt: In the planner's two-pane layout, what happens when the student taps another course?

choices.text: A new window opens beside the app
choices.why: Nothing opens; the pane updates.

choices.text: The detail replaces the list
choices.why: That is the one-pane behaviour.

choices.text: The right pane shows that course; the list stays
choices.why: Right. Only the detail side changes.

choices.text: The app switches to one pane
choices.why: Only a change of window switches the layout.

prompt: A foldable is opened while the detail of 'sql' is on screen in one pane. What must the app keep?

choices.text: The one-pane layout, so the student is not surprised
choices.why: The wider window should get two panes; the layout follows the window.

choices.text: Which course is selected
choices.why: Right. It is state: the screen on top in one pane, the highlighted row in two.

choices.text: The size of the window before it opened
choices.why: That size is gone; the app reads the new one.

choices.text: The back stack exactly as it was
choices.why: In two panes there is no detail to go back from, so the stack changes with the layout.

prompt: Which facts does Android report about a fold or hinge, according to its documentation? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Whether the device is flat or half open
choices.why: The state: FLAT or HALF_OPENED.

choices.text: Whether the fold runs horizontally or vertically
choices.why: The orientation of the fold.

choices.text: The exact angle of the hinge in degrees
choices.why: The documentation says the angle is not exposed.

choices.text: Whether it divides the window into two areas
choices.why: isSeparating.

prompt: A foldable half open with the fold horizontal, like a small laptop, is in the ___ posture.
In the program's output, which window gets two panes?

choices.text: phone, landscape (800 x 360)
choices.why: Medium wide and compact tall: one pane.

choices.text: tablet, portrait (800 x 1280)
choices.why: 800 dp is medium width: one pane.

choices.text: desktop window, short (1000 x 420)
choices.why: Wide enough, but compact tall: one pane.

choices.text: foldable, open, landscape (880 x 700)
choices.why: Right. Expanded wide and medium tall.

prompt: Why does the lesson stress that the nine window sizes are examples?

choices.text: Because Node.js has no screen to measure
choices.why: True, but the reason given is about what the numbers claim.

choices.text: Because size classes change each year
choices.why: The breakpoints are documented; the windows are the made-up part.

choices.text: Round numbers, not measurements of devices
choices.why: Right. A real device of each kind can land in a different class.

choices.text: Because iOS uses the same numbers
choices.why: iOS does not publish its classes as numbers.

prompt: Order these example windows by width class, narrowest class first.
items: tablet, half in split screen (640 dp)

prompt: A new window arrives: 900 dp wide and 500 dp tall. What does the planner's rule show?

choices.text: Two panes
choices.why: Right. 900 is expanded width and 500 is medium height.

choices.text: One pane, because 500 dp is compact height
choices.why: Compact height ends at 480 dp; 500 is medium.

choices.text: One pane, because it is not a tablet
choices.why: The rule never asks about the device.

choices.text: Two panes only after a restart
choices.why: The layout follows the window as it changes.

prompt: In one pane, back from a course's detail returns to the list. What does back do from the same course in two panes?

choices.text: It closes the detail pane and shows one pane
choices.why: The layout depends on the window, not on back.

choices.text: It returns to the list, as in one pane
choices.why: The list never left, so there is no going back to it.

choices.text: It reloads the course from the server
choices.why: Back is navigation, not a refresh.

choices.text: Nothing: the list is already there
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10 is about what back does then.

prompt: Below how many dp of height does Android call a window's height compact?
Which question should a layout ask, according to both platforms' guidance?

choices.text: Which device model is this?
choices.why: Both say not to decide layout from the device.

choices.text: How much space does my window have now?
choices.why: Right, asked again whenever the window changes.

choices.text: How many pixels does the screen have?
choices.why: Pixels are lesson 7's trap; and the screen is not the window.

choices.text: Is the phone in portrait?
choices.why: Orientation does not say how much space there is.

prompt: An app's course detail is a single short card. A colleague proposes two panes from medium width instead of expanded. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: Wrong: two panes are reserved for expanded and wider
choices.why: Nothing reserves them; the breakpoint is the app's decision.

choices.text: Reasonable, if the app decides it once and writes it down
choices.why: Right. The planner splits at expanded because its detail needs room.

choices.text: Wrong: medium windows cannot show a list
choices.why: They can; one pane is a list too.

choices.text: Right, but only on iOS
choices.why: The rule is about the window, on either platform.

prompt: In split screen, the size class comes from the app's ___, not from the device's screen.
